title: India's NRI Deposit Drive May Hit $70 Billion as Banks Shatter 2013 Record in Just 45 Days
excerpt: SBI Research sharply raises FCNR(B) projections as total RBI-linked forex inflows could reach $85 billion, potentially swinging India's balance of payments to a $50 billion surplus.
body:
• SBI Research has raised its FCNR(B) deposit projection to $65–70 billion, up from an earlier estimate of $40–45 billion, with total RBI-linked inflows potentially reaching $80–85 billion.
  • Banks have already raised more in 45 days than the entire $26 billion mobilised during the 2013 FCNR scheme, which ran for nearly three months.
  • NRI deposit rates are now as high as 6.5% on US dollar deposits, with leveraged returns potentially exceeding 20% for high-net-worth investors.
  • The RBI's concessional swap window, which absorbs banks' hedging costs, remains open until September 30.

Breaking the 2013 Record

India's push to attract foreign currency deposits from non-resident Indians is gathering momentum far faster than anyone expected. SBI Research now projects that FCNR(B) deposits alone could reach $65–70 billion by the time the Reserve Bank of India's concessional swap scheme closes on September 30 — a sharp upward revision from its earlier estimate of $40–45 billion.

The pace is remarkable. According to RBI data, FCNR(B) deposits had reached $17.41 billion as of July 17, with total inflows under the special swap window standing at $20.72 billion. SBI Research estimates deposits may have climbed further to $26–28 billion by July 23, meaning banks have already surpassed the entire $26 billion raised during a similar RBI initiative in 2013 — and they did it in roughly 45 days, compared to three months the last time around.

RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra confirmed the momentum during a recent briefing. "Obviously, most of it is coming through FCNR(B) deposits," he said, adding that government securities have also attracted over $7 billion in inflows since the June 5 policy announcements.

"At this pace, the total inflows are likely to be robust."

— Sanjay Malhotra, RBI Governor

What's Driving the Rush

The mechanics are straightforward but powerful. On June 5, the RBI announced it would absorb the full foreign exchange hedging cost on fresh FCNR(B) deposits of three to five years — effectively reducing banks' cost to zero and allowing them to offer substantially higher interest rates to NRI depositors.

Several major banks moved quickly. ICICI Bank now offers 6.50% on NRI fixed deposits. State Bank of India launched an Advantage FCNR(B) scheme with rates up to 6% for five-year tenures. Bank of Baroda, HDFC Bank, and Kotak Mahindra Bank followed with similarly elevated rates across US dollar, British pound, Euro, and Canadian dollar deposits.

For NRIs, these rates compare favourably to current US Treasury yields of around 4.20% for three-year bonds. But the real attraction for wealthy depositors goes beyond headline rates. According to calculations by Emkay Global Financial Services, an investor putting in $1 million and leveraging it nine times could generate annual returns of about $220,000 — a return of 21.8% on the original investment. Even at more conservative leverage of three times, returns work out to 11.6%.

Balance of Payments Impact

The flood of foreign currency is reshaping India's external position. Including Overseas Foreign Currency Borrowings and External Commercial Borrowings, SBI Research expects total inflows under the RBI measures to reach $80–85 billion. If that materialises, it could push India's balance of payments to a surplus of over $50 billion in FY27 — a dramatic reversal from an earlier projected deficit of $65–70 billion.

The rupee has already felt the effect. Analysts suggest the currency could strengthen to around 92 per dollar, and bank deposit growth could jump to 14.5%, with the credit-deposit gap shrinking to less than 2% from its peak of 6.7% in FY24.

RBI Governor Malhotra dismissed concerns about recirculation — the risk that existing deposits are being recycled to capture higher yields. "We do not find any prima facie evidence of recirculation of the existing deposits, in whatever form, to be of any significance or concern," he said.

What NRIs Should Know

The FCNR(B) window remains open until September 30, while ECB and OFCB windows close on December 31. Most existing FCNR deposits maturing in August and September are expected to renew under the new scheme, given the significantly higher rates on offer. The RBI has also clarified that banks can extend loans to non-residents against these deposits, adding another layer of flexibility for NRI investors looking to participate.
